chapter.title: Rendering Large Lists
chapter.description: The one optimisation that reliably matters, plus splitting work at the bundle level.

blocks.text: Thousands of DOM nodes are slow no matter how well your components are written. **Virtualisation** renders only the rows currently visible, plus a small buffer.

blocks.caption: Ten thousand items, roughly twenty DOM nodes.

blocks.text: Virtualisation turns a list that janks into one that scrolls smoothly, and it is one of the few optimisations whose benefit grows with your data. Reach for it before micro-optimising row components.
The fastest component is one that was never downloaded. `lazy` and `Suspense` split a route or a heavy widget into its own chunk, fetched on demand.

items: Split at route boundaries first - that is where the biggest wins are.
Split heavy dependencies such as chart, editor and map libraries.
Do not split tiny components: an extra network request costs more than the bytes saved.
Measure. Network and Performance tabs first, then the React Profiler.
Reduce the bundle: code split routes and heavy libraries.
Move state down, or lift content up, to shrink what re-renders.
Only then apply `memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback`, and verify each one helped.

blocks.title: Write a simple memoisation helper
blocks.instructions: Complete memoize so it caches the result per argument and only calls fn once per distinct value.

tests.name: It returns the right result
tests.code: var f = memoize(function (n) { return n * 2; }); return f(4) === 8;

tests.name: Repeated calls hit the cache
tests.code: var n = 0; var f = memoize(function (x) { n++; return x; }); f(1); f(1); f(1); return n === 1;

tests.name: Different arguments are computed separately
tests.code: var n = 0; var f = memoize(function (x) { n++; return x; }); f(1); f(2); return n === 2;

previous.title: useMemo and useCallback
previous.description: What each one caches, when it pays off, and what it costs.

blocks.text: `useMemo` caches a **value**. `useCallback` caches a **function**. Both recompute when their dependencies change and both exist to keep something stable between renders.

items: The calculation is genuinely expensive - sorting thousands of rows, parsing a large payload.
The result is passed to a memoised child or used as an effect dependency, so its identity matters.

blocks.text: If neither applies, you are adding a dependency array to maintain and a cache to hold for no benefit.
Memoisation is not free. It allocates memory, runs a dependency comparison every render, and adds a dependency array that can go stale. Wrapping everything makes an app slower and harder to change.

The React Compiler analyses your components and inserts memoisation automatically. Where it is enabled, most manual `useMemo` and `useCallback` calls become unnecessary - which is another good reason not to scatter them by hand today.
